one_liner: This paper introduces 'apparent complexity' as a measure that captures the non-monotonic rise and fall of structure in closed systems, using a coffee-cream cellular automaton to show complexity peaks before equilibrium.
paragraphs: The paper addresses a long-standing intuition in physics: while entropy always increases in closed systems, complexity—defined as the richness of structure or information content—appears to rise first and then decline. For example, the universe started simple after the Big Bang, developed stars and galaxies over time, and will end in a featureless heat death. The authors use the mixing of coffee and cream as an intuitive model to explore why systems become more complex before reaching equilibrium, challenging the idea that entropy alone captures all aspects of system behavior.

To quantify complexity, they propose 'apparent complexity': the Kolmogorov complexity of a coarse-grained snapshot of the system, which captures meaningful patterns without requiring full microscopic detail. They simulate a 2D cellular automaton where coffee and cream particles either interact or remain non-interacting. By analyzing how the compressed description length of these coarse-grained states evolves over time, they isolate the effect of interactions on structure formation—using numerical experiments to test whether complexity peaks during mixing.

The results show that when particles do not interact, apparent complexity remains low throughout; but with interactions, complexity rises to a peak comparable to the cup’s width before declining as uniformity sets in. This provides the first numerical evidence that complexity can peak mid-entropy-increase, supporting theoretical conjectures. The paper raises the open challenge of proving this behavior analytically and suggests that apparent complexity could be a useful tool for studying self-organization in cosmology, biology, and other complex systems where structure emerges transiently.
key_takeaways: Complexity in closed systems can increase before decreasing, unlike entropy which rises monotonically.
Apparent complexity—Kolmogorov complexity of coarse-grained states—is proposed as a practical measure for capturing structural richness.
Interactions between particles are essential for complexity to emerge; non-interacting systems remain simple.
Numerical simulations of a coffee-cream automaton show complexity peaks at intermediate times, matching real-world observations.
This work opens the door to formalizing a 'complexity principle' for closed systems, with implications beyond physics.
eli5: Imagine you pour cream into coffee—it starts as two separate layers (simple), then gets swirls and patterns (super interesting!), and finally becomes one even color again (boring). This paper shows that the swirls are the most complex part, and it’s like the system gets ‘busy’ before it calms down.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of entropy and thermodynamics
Familiarity with cellular automata and Kolmogorov complexity
applications: Modeling structure formation in cosmology, such as galaxy evolution before heat death
Improving algorithms for detecting patterns in noisy data or time-series systems
title: The Coffee Automaton
